articles.title: Sharpe Ratios, Inflation Anchors, and Thin Compensation - https://www.connectmoney.com/
articles.summary: Sharpe Ratios, Inflation Anchors, and Thin Compensation  https://www.connectmoney.com/
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary
The repricing of the U.S. yield curve has changed the near-term rate outlook without materially altering long-run inflation expectations. In the United States, the markets are pricing roughly another 50-75 basis points of tightening over the next 12 months, while the implied long-horizon inflation rate remains close to 2.06%. That distinction matters as higher nominal yields have not created a compelling case for long-dated bonds if investors are receiving only modest compensation for real-rate, inflation and duration risk.
Using an interest-rate-curve framework that separates the market’s expected path for short rates from compensation for bearing duration risk, the implied Sharpe ratio for U.S. nominal rate exposure is only 0.12. That is an improvement from 0.10 in June 2025 but remains a thin reward for accepting potentially significant bond volatility at the long end. The preferred positioning may be selective inflation-protected duration and caution toward long nominal exposure.
U.S. Curve Reprices Higher
The U.S. yield curve has undergone a dramatic shift. Fifteen months ago, the curve was inverted through roughly three years and embedded expectations for about 50 basis points of Fed easing. By early this week, the six-month rate stood near 4.30%, while the three-year rate was roughly 63 basis points higher. The market had moved from expecting cuts to pricing roughly 50 basis points of tightening.
The Federal Reserve reinforced that shift on Sept. 16, raising its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75% to 4.00%, the first increase since 2023. The Fed’s median projection implied a policy rate of about 4.125% at year-end, consistent with one further quarter-point increase.
Further out the curve, the increase has been more contained. The 30-year dollar swap rate, for example, rose about 56 basis points from the earlier comparison point, while the estimated long-horizon expected short rate rose only 26 basis points to 4.11%. The message is that the market has primarily repriced the next several years of policy and growth, not permanently reset its view of where nominal rates will settle.
Inflation Expectations Remain Anchored
The implied long-run U.S. real short rate is about 2.05%, leaving expected long-term inflation near 2.06%. That is effectively unchanged from the 2.1% estimated in June 2025.
Other measures show a somewhat higher but still relatively contained inflation outlook. The Cleveland Fed’s 10-year expected inflation measure stood at 2.57% as of this week, while its 30-year estimate was 2.61%. Those measures incorporate model-based estimates of inflation and risk premia, and are not directly comparable with the swap-curve calculation. Still, neither suggests that investors have abandoned confidence in the Fed’s long-run inflation objective.
The distinction between realized inflation and long-run expected inflation is central. Inflation can remain elevated in current data while long-term market pricing stays anchored. The risk in owning long nominal bonds is therefore not just a renewed inflation shock; it is also a rise in real yields driven by stronger growth, higher productivity expectations, persistent fiscal borrowing needs or a higher estimate of the neutral policy rate.
Thin Compensation for Duration
The curve-implied Sharpe ratio of 0.12 means the market offers only a modest excess return per unit of expected interest-rate volatility for holding U.S. nominal duration. In more tangible terms, roughly 42 basis points of the 10-year par dollar swap rate reflects compensation for taking interest-rate risk.
That compares with 62 basis points in sterling, 56 basis points in yen and 26 basis points in euro rates. The figures do not mean long bonds cannot rally. Rather, they suggest the risk premium embedded in long-end nominal rates is too limited to justify a large strategic overweight when rate volatility remains elevated and real yields can still rise.
The real-rate calculation is more striking. The Sharpe ratio for U.S. inflation-protected rate risk is estimated at 0.10, close to that of nominal bonds. For long-term investors whose liabilities are linked to real spending power, inflation-linked bonds more directly match the underlying objective: they protect purchasing power rather than requiring an investor to separately bear inflation uncertainty.
Portfolio Implications
A 0.12 Sharpe ratio does not support a broad, aggressive allocation to long nominal U.S. bonds. Therefore, maintaining short-to-intermediate maturity exposure for carry and liquidity, and adding long duration gradually rather than making a single large directional bet makes sense.
The global fixed-income opportunity set has improved because absolute yields are higher. But higher yields alone do not make every bond attractive. The current curve pricing argues for discipline, perhaps owning long-term rate exposure in inflation-protected form where possible and demand more compensation before accepting long nominal duration.
We want to hear your views.
Has the bond market become more attractive, or has it simply become more volatile?

articles.title: Dollar and Euro Exchange Rates Drop in Cuba: Informal Market Shows Continued Decline - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Dollar and Euro Exchange Rates Drop in Cuba: Informal Market Shows Continued Decline  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
On Wednesday, October 7th, at 10:00 a.m. local time, Cuba's informal currency exchange market opened with both the U.S. dollar and the euro losing ground against the Cuban peso. The U.S. dollar fell to 768 CUP, the euro declined to 864 CUP, while the MLC (Moneda Libremente Convertible) stood at an indicative value of 598 CUP, though data for this time slot is limited.
Fluctuations in the U.S. Dollar
The U.S. dollar is currently valued at 768 Cuban pesos (CUP) in the informal market, with buying and selling rates at 760 CUP and 775 CUP, respectively. This marks a decrease of 2 pesos from the previous session, where it closed at approximately 770 CUP. Over the past week, the dollar has gained 14 pesos from 754 CUP, a 1.9% increase. When compared to the 30-day mark, the current rate is 85 pesos higher than the 683 CUP recorded a month ago, though this change might partially reflect adjustments in the index methodology. Throughout the past month, the dollar has ranged from a low of 683 CUP to a high of 785 CUP, continuing to set the pace in the informal market amidst a severe foreign currency shortage.
Current Euro Trends
The euro stands at 864 CUP, with a buying rate of 850 CUP and a selling rate of 878 CUP. Compared to the previous day, the euro has dropped by 6 pesos from 870 CUP, a 0.7% decline. Weekly, the euro has remained relatively stable, changing just 1 peso from 863 CUP a week ago. Over the last 30 days, it has increased by 88.5 pesos from 776 CUP, although caution is advised as this comparison may include methodological adjustments. In the past month, the euro fluctuated between 776 CUP and 885 CUP, remaining the most expensive currency in Cuba's parallel market, exceeding the dollar's rate by 96 pesos.
MLC Exchange Observations
The MLC shows an indicative value of 598 CUP, with a buying rate of 498 CUP and a selling rate of 698 CUP. Given the limited data during this hour, this figure should be approached with caution. The MLC has risen by 5 pesos from 593 CUP the previous day. Over the last week, its value increased by 103.5 pesos from 495 CUP, a 20.9% rise, and over 30 days, it's up by 176.5 pesos from 422 CUP, a 41.9% increase, though these changes may partly reflect methodological index adjustments. The MLC, lacking physical presence, is primarily used in state stores that accept it, limiting its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rate Overview
USD to CUP exchange rate: 768 CUP. EUR to CUP exchange rate: 864 CUP. MLC to CUP exchange rate: 598 CUP (indicative, limited data).
Disparity Between Informal and Official Rates
The official exchange rate from Cuba's Central Bank (Segment III) remains at 695 CUP per dollar and 779 CUP per euro, significantly lower than the rates prevailing in everyday informal market transactions. The disparity surpasses 73 pesos for the dollar and 85 pesos for the euro.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rate remains far from the informal market's and fails to meet the population's real currency demands. Over the past month, the official dollar rate rose from 640 to 695 CUP, and the euro from 744 to 779 CUP, without closing the gap with the parallel market.
Informal Market Dynamics
The gap between official and informal rates highlights the persistent currency shortage within the state banking system and the high demand for dollars and euros among Cubans, whether for emigration, importing goods, safeguarding savings, or private sector purchases.
In a context of sustained inflation, low state salaries, and growing partial dollarization of the economy, any variation in the informal market directly impacts domestic prices and Cubans' purchasing power.
Methodology Behind Exchange Rates
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate Index is derived from analyzing thousands of currency trading posts on Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation excludes atypical offers and spam, weighs each operation by its age, and consolidates a representative value updated several times daily.
U.S. Dollar (USD) to Cuban Peso (CUP) equivalency, according to the exchange rates on Wednesday, October 7, 2026: 1 USD = 768 CUP, 5 USD = 3,840 CUP, 10 USD = 7,680 CUP, 20 USD = 15,360 CUP, 50 USD = 38,400 CUP, 100 USD = 76,800 CUP.
Euro (EUR) to Cuban Peso (CUP) equivalency, according to the exchange rates on Wednesday, October 7, 2026: 1 EUR = 864 CUP, 5 EUR = 4,320 CUP, 10 EUR = 8,640 CUP, 20 EUR = 17,280 CUP, 50 EUR = 43,200 CUP, 100 EUR = 86,400 CUP, 200 EUR = 172,800 CUP.
Understanding the Informal Currency Market in Cuba
Why is there a disparity between the official and informal exchange rates in Cuba?
The disparity is primarily due to a significant shortage of foreign currencies in the state banking system and high demand among the Cuban population for dollars and euros. This demand arises from needs related to emigration, importing goods, safeguarding savings, or making purchases in the private sector.
How does the informal market impact Cuba's economy?
The informal market significantly affects Cuba's economy by influencing domestic prices and the purchasing power of Cubans. This impact is especially pronounced in a context of sustained inflation, low state salaries, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy.

articles.full_text:
The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond surged to its highest level since 2002, as renewed concerns over inflation and the U.S. government's fiscal burden fueled a broad selloff in global bond markets.
The 30-year Treasury yield rose as high as 5.7041% at one point on the 7th, its highest in 24 years, according to Reuters. The selloff in long-dated Treasurys continued ahead of the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve's September Federal Open Market Committee meeting, scheduled for that afternoon.
The selloff in global bond markets, which had eased somewhat the previous day, also regained strength. Analysts said rising price pressures and concerns over widening fiscal deficits and expanded bond issuance by major governments are pushing long-term yields higher.
A renewed rise in international oil prices added to the pressure on bond markets. Brent crude futures traded at around $101.54 a barrel, up more than 1% from the previous session. Higher oil prices raise inflationary pressure and can limit central banks' room to cut interest rates, making them a factor behind rising bond yields.
Market participants are also watching the 10-year Treasury auction scheduled for the same day and the 30-year auction set for the 8th. The two auctions are expected to serve as a test of how aggressively investors will buy long-dated U.S. government debt even at elevated yield levels.
The recent rise in long-term Treasury yields comes amid growing wariness about the massive U.S. fiscal deficit and mounting government debt. Analysts said investors are demanding higher yields as expectations of continued increases in long-dated bond supply combine with inflation concerns.
Short-term yields also jumped. The two-year Treasury yield rose as high as 4.8143% during the session, up 0.0168 percentage point from the previous trading day, according to foreign news reports. The 30-year yield remained above 5.7%, however, preserving a normal yield curve in which long-term rates exceed short-term rates.
French government bond yields also rose. The French 10-year yield traded at 4.8536%, up 9.88 basis points from the previous day. French bond yields had fallen 9 basis points after Marine Le Pen, a leading French presidential contender, said she would strengthen state finances by cutting public spending, but they rebounded on the day.

articles.summary: ECB's Dolenc says the ECB is not responsible for fiscal policy  Newsquawk
articles.full_text:
Context
Statements of this kind sit in the long-running fiscal-monetary division of labour debate inside the euro area, where central bankers periodically remind governments that deficit and debt management is a sovereign competence, not something the Governing Council will underwrite. The remark typically surfaces when spread widening or heavy supply is pulling the central bank toward intervention questions, and the signal is a refusal to pre-commit support. The relevant channel is the sovereign spread complex rather than the policy rate itself: such comments have historically been read as reinforcing conditionality around backstop tools, which matters most for the higher-beta periphery where the transmission protection narrative underpins valuations. The distinction worth drawing is between a generic restatement of mandates, which tends to fade quickly, and pushback timed to a specific fiscal loosening or issuance event, which has more durable spread implications. Worth watching is whether other officials echo the line and whether it precedes any discussion of bond-buying conditionality, since clustered commentary has been the tell rather than a single voice.

articles.title: IMF Chief Warns of Soaring Long-Term Bond Yields in Japan and United States - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: IMF Chief Warns of Soaring Long-Term Bond Yields in Japan and United States  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has expressed acute concern over the rapid ascent of long-term interest rates in Japan and the United States, warning that deteriorating fiscal conditions and ballooning public debt threaten to destabilize the broader global economy.
Speaking in Singapore on Wednesday, October 7, ahead of the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group scheduled for Bangkok next week, Georgieva highlighted a synchronized spike in sovereign borrowing costs that reflects deepening structural pressures in the world's largest advanced economies.
Three-Decade Highs in Japanese Yields
The IMF chief noted that the 10-year Japanese government bond yield has reached its highest level in approximately thirty years. This milestone marks a definitive rupture from Japan's prolonged era of ultra-loose monetary policy and deflationary stagnation. As the Bank of Japan continues its cautious normalization process, moving away from negative interest rates and yield curve control, the market is repricing the long-term cost of capital in a country that holds one of the highest public debt-to-gross domestic product ratios in the developed world.
Georgieva described the recent interest rate hikes orchestrated by central banks in Japan, the United States, and Europe as "highly appropriate" given the prevailing macroeconomic data. However, she cautioned that the 10-year US Treasury yield has simultaneously hit its highest level in roughly nineteen years, with both benchmarks "still climbing." The concurrent rise in long-term rates across the Pacific suggests that global capital markets are demanding higher risk premiums to compensate for persistent inflation and expansive fiscal deficits.
Fiscal Deterioration and Inflation Drivers
Beyond the immediate mechanics of monetary tightening, the IMF's warning centers on the fiscal trajectory of major economies. Georgieva argued that the current situation "demands an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses" to address the unsustainable accumulation of public debt. When long-term yields climb, the cost of servicing existing and newly issued sovereign debt rises in tandem, crowding out productive public investment and exacerbating deficit spirals.
Compounding these fiscal vulnerabilities is a new inflationary dynamic. Georgieva pointed to a global energy price shock stemming from ongoing turmoil in the Middle East, which she characterized as "large but contained." More structurally, she warned that an investment boom linked to artificial intelligence and rising resource prices are actively fueling inflation. The massive capital expenditure required to build AI infrastructure, including energy-intensive data centers, is driving up demand for copper, electricity, and specialized hardware, embedding upward price pressures into the global supply chain.
Policy Divergence and Global Spillovers
The divergence in monetary policy cycles between major economies complicates the global outlook. While the US Federal Reserve has maintained a restrictive stance to quell stubborn services inflation, the Bank of Japan is raising rates from a near-zero baseline to defend the yen and normalize domestic price dynamics. This divergence creates volatile currency fluctuations and capital flow disruptions, particularly for emerging markets that borrow in dollars or yen.
The nineteen-year peak in US Treasury yields transports bond markets back to the pre-2008 financial crisis environment, a period characterized by vastly different global growth dynamics and debt loads. Today, the United States faces a structural deficit widened by recent legislative spending packages and tax policies, forcing the Treasury to issue record volumes of long-dated bonds to finance the gap. When the supply of Treasuries outpaces institutional demand, yields must rise to attract marginal buyers, a dynamic that directly impacts global mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, and equity valuations.
In Japan, the structural challenge is demographic. An aging and shrinking population naturally suppresses domestic demand and tax revenues, making the servicing of a debt burden exceeding 250 percent of gross domestic product highly sensitive to interest rate movements. The Bank of Japan's transition away from its yield curve control mechanism was designed to be gradual, but global bond market volatility has frequently forced Tokyo to intervene in currency markets to prevent excessive yen depreciation, which imports inflation through higher energy and food costs.
Georgieva's reference to the artificial intelligence investment boom highlights a supply-side constraint that central banks struggle to manage through traditional demand-side interest rate tools. The physical infrastructure required for generative AI, particularly advanced semiconductor fabrication and power generation, requires immense capital and raw materials. As sovereign wealth funds and private equity pour trillions into this sector, the resulting competition for resources creates localized inflation hotspots that bleed into broader consumer price indices.
Furthermore, the geopolitical fragmentation of global trade continues to impose efficiency costs that manifest as structural inflation. The rerouting of supply chains away from traditional low-cost manufacturing hubs toward allied nations, a process often termed friend-shoring, inherently raises the baseline cost of goods. When combined with the Middle East energy shock, which threatens critical maritime chokepoints, the inflationary floor remains stubbornly high regardless of short-term fluctuations in consumer demand.
As finance ministers and central bank governors prepare to convene in Bangkok, the IMF's mandate will focus heavily on coordinating fiscal consolidation without triggering a synchronized growth slowdown. Georgieva's remarks signal that the Fund views the current yield environment not merely as a market correction, but as a fundamental repricing of sovereign risk in an era of geopolitical fragmentation, demographic aging, and technological disruption.
The immediate test for policymakers will be demonstrating a credible commitment to fiscal discipline. Without clear pathways to stabilize debt trajectories, central banks may be forced to keep policy rates elevated for longer, increasing the risk of a credit contraction that could tip fragile economies into recession. The Bangkok meetings are expected to yield new frameworks for debt transparency and cross-border financial resilience, though the political will to implement unpopular fiscal adjustments remains the primary obstacle to stabilizing long-term global yields.

articles.title: DM Yield Curves and 2yr to Policy Rate Spreads - Continuum Economics
articles.summary: DM Yield Curves and 2yr to Policy Rate Spreads  Continuum Economics
articles.full_text:
· The scale of the September yield rise was driven mainly policy rate tightening ideas and an extra real yield premium. However, the rise in bond volatility, plus the role of speculative funds appears to have amplified the move. Moderate or major bond positive news could see a partial correction in the yield rise, though 10yr JGB yields could be the exception given the excessive supply from huge BOJ QT. While we also see 2027 tightening fears as overdone, this is unlikely to be rethought until the key December Fed/ECB and BOJ meetings.
We have previously highlighted some of the forces driving up government bond yields (here), but could this have gone too far in recent weeks?
Figure 1: Big DM 10-2yr Yield Curve – Last 12 Months (%)
Source: Datastream/Continuum Economics
In the September DM Rates outlook (here), we argued that the main forces driving government bond yields higher had been a rethink on prospective policy rates and some extra real yield premium at the long-end of the curve. Looking at 10-2yr Big DM yield curves (Figure 1) over the past 12 months shows no major yield curve steepening except for Japan. Taking a long-term perspective (Figure 2), 10-2yr yield curves in the 1993-2007 period were steeper than currently – the 2008-2021 period occasionally had steep yield curves but with abnormally low 2yr and policy rates.
Figure 2: Big DM 10-2yr Yield Curve – The Long Term (%)
Source: Datastream/Continuum Economics
Japan 10-2yr yield curve is however is relatively steep, despite money market discounting 75bps of BOJ hikes in by end 2027. We continue to point out that BOJ QT is excessive at 6% of GDP (Figure 3) and is causing excess supply pressures compare to other major DM government bond markets (here). It is also worth remembering that though the U.S. budget deficit is excessive and unlikely to be corrected after the mid-term elections, the Fed is growing bond holdings in line with currency in circulation and nominal GDP in contrast to other DM central banks.
Figure 3: Big DM Budget Deficits and QT (% of GDP)
Source: Continuum Economics
Meanwhile, looking at 2yr-policy rate spread shows that the front-end could have discounted too much tightening from the Fed, ECB and BOE. In the U.S., money markets are discounting 25bps hikes in December, March and June 2027. If the Fed hike in December, but dampen 2027 rate hike ideas it could cause a decline in 2yr U.S. Treasuries (Figure 4 shows that the end of mini tightening cycles normally see a narrowing of 2yr-policy rate). Near-term if the September core CPI is controlled, then it could reinforce the idea that the Fed will hold in October and may not hike after December. For 2 and 10yr yields, it also worth noting that crude oil flows through the Straits of Hormuz are improving (as Iran effectiveness is lower) and this is helping temper crude oil prices. Finally, the scale of the selloff in U.S. Treasuries has been amplified by the spike in volatility and also the reduced quality of long-term U.S. holders as hedge funds hold more Treasuries. If an economic catalyst is seen, this can produce a partial reverse of the September yield rise – partial as the market needs to see the Fed dots in December to decide on 2027 policy prospects.
Figure 4: 2yr U.S. Treasury to Fed Funds Policy Spread Versus Inverted Fed Funds Rate (%)
Source: Datastream/Continuum Economics
In the EZ, 25bps hikes are only fully discounted in Feb 4 and April 29 2027 ECB meetings, as the French fiscal tensions have tightened financial conditions in some countries. Though more hopes exist of the 2027 French budget passing than 2025 or 2026 (here), French fiscal and political uncertainty will remain into 2027. Additionally, EZ wage inflation is consistent with the 2% target, while 2nd round effects from the Iran war remain unlikely. This could mean that the 2yr policy spread to ECB depo rate is too high and the market reduces the scale of tightening discounted. In turn this could ripple across the curve to reduce the scale of tension at the long-end. This is more likely at the December 17 rather than the October 29 ECB meeting. However, 10yr real Bund yields are lower than the U.S./UK and this is likely to be a modest correction lower in yields.
Figure 5: 2yr Bund to ECB Depo Rate Spread Versus Inverted ECB Policy Rate (%)
Source: Datastream/Continuum Economics
Finally, JGB’s are discounting 25bps BOJ rate hikes in December, April and October 2027. However, the BOJ have not given any signs that they will accelerate the slow pace of policy rate normalisation and we see the next 25bps hike coming at the March or April 2027 BOJ meeting (here). This could mean 2yr JGB yields come down in Q1 2027 though not sooner. Meanwhile, we fear that BOJ QT (Figure 2) is so large that it could cause a further spike higher in 10yr JGB yields to 3.25-3.50%, which could spill over via yield competition to some DM 10yr yields.

articles.title: Silver Price Forecast: XAG/USD ticks lower to near $60.60 as US bond yields bounce back - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: Silver Price Forecast: XAG/USD ticks lower to near $60.60 as US bond yields bounce back  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
Silver price (XAG/USD) is slightly down to near $60.60 during the European trading session on Wednesday. The white metal faces marginal selling pressure as United States (US) Treasury Yields regain ground after a corrective move the previous day.
10-year US Treasury Yields are up 0.4% at 5.31%, at press time, close to their two-decade high of 5.35% posted last week.
Higher yields on US-backed securities diminish the appeal of non-yielding assets, such as Silver.
A recovery move in US bond yields has also lend support to the US Dollar. As of writing, the US Dollar Index (DXY), which gauges the Greenback’s value against six major currencies, trades 0.33% higher at around 102.18.
Technically, a higher US Dollar makes the Silver price an unfavorable risk-reward bet for investors.
It seems that the return of buying interest in oil prices has staged a recovery in United States (US) Treasury Yields. The WTI Oil price has shown some signs of reversal from its monthly low of $86.32 posted on Tuesday. Energy products attract bids amid fears that a storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico would become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and would likely hit oil and gas producing facilities, Reuters report.
Analysts at Danske Bank have highlighted that US bond yields are in a longer-term uptrend not only supply of Treasuries but also from the hyperscalers. Against this setting, the bank cautions that “we do see the risk of 10Y and 30Y Treasuries hitting 6% as investors demand a higher premium for the long end,” underscoring concerns that term premia may need to rise further to clear upcoming issuance.
In the daily chart, XAG/USD trades at $60.60, keeping a bearish near-term tone as it holds below the 20-day exponential moving average (EMA) at $62.71. The downside bias is reinforced by the Relative Strength Index (RSI) near 40, which suggests subdued bullish momentum and leaves the metal vulnerable to further weakness while it remains capped beneath the nearby EMA resistance.
On the topside, immediate resistance is located at the 20-day EMA at $62.71, and a sustained break above this level would be needed to ease the current bearish pressure and open the door for a more constructive recovery. On the downside, the October 2 low near 59.70 is the key support zone.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)
Silver is a precious metal highly traded among investors. It has been historically used as a store of value and a medium of exchange. Although less popular than Gold, traders may turn to Silver to diversify their investment portfolio, for its intrinsic value or as a potential hedge during high-inflation periods. Investors can buy physical Silver, in coins or in bars, or trade it through vehicles such as Exchange Traded Funds, which track its price on international markets.
Silver prices can move due to a wide range of factors. Geopolitical instability or fears of a deep recession can make Silver price escalate due to its safe-haven status, although to a lesser extent than Gold's. As a yieldless asset, Silver tends to rise with lower interest rates. Its moves also depend on how the US Dollar (USD) behaves as the asset is priced in dollars (XAG/USD). A strong Dollar tends to keep the price of Silver at bay, whereas a weaker Dollar is likely to propel prices up. Other factors such as investment demand, mining supply – Silver is much more abundant than Gold – and recycling rates can also affect prices.
Silver is widely used in industry, particularly in sectors such as electronics or solar energy, as it has one of the highest electric conductivity of all metals – more than Copper and Gold. A surge in demand can increase prices, while a decline tends to lower them. Dynamics in the US, Chinese and Indian economies can also contribute to price swings: for the US and particularly China, their big industrial sectors use Silver in various processes; in India, consumers’ demand for the precious metal for jewellery also plays a key role in setting prices.
Silver prices tend to follow Gold's moves. When Gold prices rise, Silver typically follows suit, as their status as safe-haven assets is similar. The Gold/Silver ratio, which shows the number of ounces of Silver needed to equal the value of one ounce of Gold, may help to determine the relative valuation between both metals. Some investors may consider a high ratio as an indicator that Silver is undervalued, or Gold is overvalued. On the contrary, a low ratio might suggest that Gold is undervalued relative to Silver.

articles.title: Euro-Dollar On Course for 1.10: ING - Pound Sterling Live
articles.summary: Euro-Dollar On Course for 1.10: ING  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Le Pen's alternative budget is said to be worth watching. File image. Source: Global Panorama, Flickr. Licensing: Creative Commons 2.0.
The euro could fall to $1.10 if French bond stress intensifies and ECB rate expectations keep unwinding.
The euro-to-dollar exchange rate has scope to test 1.110 and 1.100 as French bond market turbulence erodes the two supports that carried the currency through the first half of the year, according to ING Bank.
The euro started the week at the bottom of the G10 scorecard, which ING reads as confirmation that French debt remains the market's primary concern.
"The euro is being affected through two channels: a direct one, where a fiscal risk premium (so far not extreme) has been added, and an indirect one via a repricing lower in ECB rate expectations," says Francesco Pesole, FX Strategist at ING Bank.
In midweek trade, we see French bond yields rise from Tuesday's floor, with the ten-year reaching 4.847%. The euro-to-dollar conversion is down 0.60% on the day at 1.1193, reflecting renewed pressures.
Weakness comes as expectations for a rate rise at the March ECB meeting has fallen to 45 basis points from 80bp on 24 September, a repricing that has taken the two-year swap rate differential between the euro and dollar to minus 167bp.
"The last time the spread was at these levels was in August 2025. At that point, EUR/USD was trading around 1.16-1.17, but that reflected a sizeable USD-specific risk premium after Liberation Day and a sharp rise in USD hedging demand," says Pesole.
Strip that premium out and the comparison turns bearish.
"Before Liberation Day, a swap spread at current levels was consistent with EUR/USD closer to 1.08," says Pesole.
"We don't have much confidence in a sustained rebound. The fiscal risk premium is still relatively limited, leaving scope for EUR/USD to test 1.110 or even 1.100 if bond market stress intensifies," says Pesole.
EUR/USD: The Premium Has Room to Grow
The argument that the fiscal premium is contained is the one that matters for euro buyers, because a contained premium is one with room to widen.
TD Securities says the market's reaction to French concerns has stayed relatively tame against the last episode of comparable OAT-Bund widening, which leaves scope for near-term euro underperformance.
Marine Le Pen's counter-budget is the next test, with markets awaiting the detail.
The bind for the single currency is that neither outcome in Paris clearly helps it.
A budget that fails raises the fiscal premium directly, while a deterioration severe enough to bring the ECB's support tools into play suppresses the rate expectations the euro has been trading on.
EUR/USD and GBP/EUR: What It Means for Sterling
The pound reached 1.1829 against the euro on Wednesday, its best for sterling-based euro buyers since June 2025, and ING's call points to that advance having further to run.
A euro-to-dollar rate at 1.10 with the pound-to-dollar rate holding its range would put the pound-to-euro rate well into the 1.19s.
The condition attached is that the pound keeps its own house in order, with the 28 October Budget the event capable of removing sterling from the trade.
For now the euro is the weaker leg of both pairs, and Barclays expects French developments to remain the primary driver of the euro-pound cross.
Beneath the market in euro-dollar, 1.1160 is Monday's low and the gateway to ING's targets.
Above it, 1.1289 is the level the euro needs to reclaim to argue the breakdown has failed.
Christine Lagarde speaks on Wednesday, and any acknowledgement that French yields are shaping the policy path would validate the repricing ING has built its forecast on.

articles.title: Repo Rate Raised to 5.50% by RBI amid Challenging Global Uncertainty, Inflation - Moneylife
articles.summary: Repo Rate Raised to 5.50% by RBI amid Challenging Global Uncertainty, Inflation  Moneylife
articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) to 5.50%, amid a challenging global environment and shifted its monetary policy stance to calibrated tightening, signalling a clear pause in the rate-cut cycle as inflationary pressures build. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate will change t0 5.25%, while the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the bank rate will remain at 5.75%.
 
The decision was taken unanimously by the six-member monetary policy committee (MPC) at its October meeting. RBI said the combination of higher food and energy prices, renewed geopolitical tensions and volatile global crude prices had altered the inflation outlook and required a recalibration of monetary policy.
 
The central bank also made it clear that rate cuts are off the table in the near term. Going forward, policy action could be either another rate hike or a pause, depending on how inflation, growth, and underlying price pressures evolve. 
 
Announcing the outcome of the MPC meeting, RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said the sudden reescalation of the West Asia conflict in September and the consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices soured global economic sentiments and heightened financial market volatility.
 
“The West Asia conflict, tariff-related uncertainties, elevated bond yields and risks of an unwieldy correction in valuation of artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are keeping global economic sentiments edgy with risk-off sentiments on EMEs. While these factors are weighing on the domestic growth-inflation outlook adversely, the inherent resilience and strength of the Indian economy are helping navigate through these challenging times. We shall implement policies that further add to this resilience. Accordingly, we shall strive for price and financial stability as both are essential for sustainable growth in the long run,” he said.
 
Inflation Outlook Turns Less Comfortable
 
RBI's decision comes as inflation is showing signs of becoming broader after remaining relatively benign last year.
 
Headline consumer price index (CPI) inflation rose to 4.8% in August 2026 from 4.5% in July, driven largely by higher food and fuel inflation. Food price pressures have also become more widespread, with notable increases in items such as sugar and onions.
 
Core inflation, which excludes food and fuel, also moved up to 4.2% in August from 3.9%, where it had remained for three consecutive months. Core inflation excluding precious metals rose to 2.9%.
 
RBI said the broadening of price pressures is visible in inflation diffusion indicators, with the weighted share of items recording inflation above 4% rising to about 37% in August.
 
The near-term inflation outlook is being clouded by a deficient southwest monsoon, El Niño conditions and high volatility in international oil prices, Mr Malhotra said, adding the price pressures are becoming visible across a wider range of food commodities, while early signs of inflation becoming more generalised were also emerging.
 
Against this backdrop, RBI has projected CPI inflation at 5.2% for FY26-27, with inflation expected at 4.9% in the second quarter, 6% in the third quarter and 5.7% in the fourth quarter.
 
Core inflation is projected at 4.4% for the financial year.
 
The governor said headline CPI inflation is expected to average almost 5.8% over the next three quarters, while core inflation is projected at 4.4% for the year.
 
Rate Cuts Off the Table
 
The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. "It only signals that, given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term, and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of the rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second-round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses," RBI said. 
 
At the same time, it acknowledged that supply-side shocks can feed into inflation expectations and corporate pricing behaviour over time.
 
The central bank said monetary policy cannot directly eliminate supply shocks, but it has to prevent them from becoming entrenched through second-round effects.
 
“Given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause,” Mr Malhotra said.
 
The extent and duration of any further tightening will depend on actual growth and inflation developments, particularly underlying inflation, the broadening of price pressures and whether supply shocks begin to influence pricing behaviour more persistently.
 
According to Dipti Deshpande, senior director and principal economist at Crisil Ltd, since the last policy review, oil prices have risen by about 40%, monsoon-related risks have materialised, domestic growth has surprised on the upside, liquidity conditions have eased significantly, and global monetary tightening has accelerated.
"The upward revisions to growth and inflation forecasts, the rate action and change in monetary policy stance help align market expectations with evolving macroeconomic realities. Alongside, the central bank is expected to remain committed to maintaining orderly liquidity and financial conditions as the economy enters the festive season. We see room for another rate hike of 25bps in December," she said.
 
Rajani Sinha, chief economist at CareEdge Ratings, pointed out that the 'calibrated tightening' stance was last adopted by the MPC in October 2018 and was subsequently changed to 'neutral' in February 2019, alongside a 25bps rate cut that marked the beginning of a policy-easing cycle. "Notably, despite the adoption of a 'calibrated tightening' stance in October 2018, no further rate hike was undertaken back then. Given this historical precedent, along with the expected moderation in headline inflation from Q4 FY26-27 onwards, we continue to believe that the current hiking cycle will be shallow, with scope for another 25bps-50bps of rate hikes going forward. Policy tightening should also provide support to the rupee, particularly against the backdrop of rate hikes by major global central banks."
 
Growth Remains Strong Despite Global Headwinds
 
While RBI has become more cautious about inflation, it remains relatively confident in the strength of the domestic economy.
 
India's real gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.8% in the first quarter of FY26-27, supported by resilient private consumption, strong investment activity and a positive contribution from net exports.
 
High-frequency indicators suggest economic activity has maintained momentum in the second quarter, although growth has moderated somewhat from the previous quarter, RBI said.
 
Manufacturing activity has remained resilient despite cost pressures, while services activity continues to be supported by domestic and external demand. Both manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indices remained in expansion territory during the quarter, although the pace of expansion slowed.
 
Private consumption has remained broadly resilient, particularly discretionary spending, while investment activity continues to show strength.
 
Exports have also provided support. Merchandise exports recorded higher double-digit growth during July and August, while services exports accelerated over the same period.
 
RBI, however, warned that global uncertainty, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions could weigh on domestic activity. A weak southwest monsoon combined with strong El Niño conditions could also affect the rabi crop and rural demand.
 
The central bank expects continued strength in non-farm activity, services and employment to support consumption. Government infrastructure spending, a revival in private capital expenditure and strong credit growth are expected to sustain investment.
 
Taking these factors into account, RBI has raised its FY26-27 GDP growth forecast by 40bps to 7.1%. It expects growth at 7.2% in Q2, 6.9% in Q3 and 6.8% in Q4. Growth in Q1 of FY27-28 is projected at 7.1%, with risks assessed as evenly balanced.
 
Global Risks Remain a Major Concern
 
RBI's more hawkish stance comes against a backdrop of renewed instability in global markets. The escalation of the West Asia conflict has pushed crude oil prices higher and increased volatility in global financial markets. The central bank said global growth is expected to slow in 2026 despite remaining resilient.
 
Rising energy and food prices are expected to push global inflation higher, potentially forcing major central banks to tighten monetary policy.
 
RBI also highlighted lingering trade uncertainty, higher government bond yields in advanced economies, and a stronger dollar as factors that are keeping global financial conditions fragile.
 
A further tightening of global financial conditions, uncertainty over the valuation of AI stocks and the unresolved West Asia conflict are identified as significant downside risks to the global economic outlook.
 
Liquidity Remains Comfortable
 
Domestic liquidity conditions have remained in surplus following measures taken to attract capital inflows, the RBI governor said.
 
Average daily surplus liquidity under the liquidity adjustment facility stood at Rs5.9 lakh crore since the previous MPC meeting in August, although liquidity was moderated in September by measures to absorb surplus funds and quarterly advance tax outflows.
 
The surplus liquidity pushed the weighted average call rate towards the lower half of the policy corridor. Short-term money market rates, including commercial paper and certificates of deposit rates, also declined significantly during August and September.
 
Government securities yields, however, hardened from mid-August amid renewed tensions in W

articles.summary: Why global liquidity is no longer moving in sync and what anshul vyas’s research shows  Zee News
articles.full_text:
Vyas’s research ultimately points toward a financial world that remains highly connected but increasingly less synchronized. Global money has not stopped moving. It is simply becoming more selective about where it goes, what risks it accepts and how long it stays.
Global money still reacts quickly to decisions made in Washington, but the consequences are becoming harder to predict.
A rise in US interest rates can weaken one currency, trigger temporary foreign selling in another market and have surprisingly little effect somewhere else. Countries may face the same external shock but experience very different financial outcomes.
That divergence is one of the questions finance and macroeconomics researcher Anshul Vyas has been examining through his work on monetary tightening, global liquidity and asset repricing across emerging and developed markets.
His research starts with a simple question: if financial markets are more connected than ever, why are they not reacting in the same way?
For years, global liquidity was often explained through a familiar pattern. When interest rates in major economies fell, borrowing became cheaper and investors searched for higher returns, often moving money toward equities and emerging markets. When monetary policy tightened, investors became more selective and some of those flows reversed.
The relationship still matters, but it does not tell the whole story.
Vyas’s work looks at what happens after the global shock reaches an individual economy.
A country with large foreign-exchange reserves, a deep domestic investor base and limited dependence on foreign borrowing may absorb tighter financial conditions differently from an economy heavily dependent on overseas capital.
The starting point may be global. The outcome increasingly depends on local financial structure.
“The same monetary shock can reach two economies and create completely different reactions,” Vyas said. “What matters is not only where the shock begins, but what kind of financial system it meets when it arrives.”
India shows why the distinction matters
India provides a useful example.
Foreign institutional investors remain influential in Indian markets, but domestic participation has grown substantially. Mutual funds, institutions and individual investors now provide a much larger source of market liquidity than in earlier periods.
That changes the way international capital movements can affect Indian assets.
When foreign investors reduce exposure, domestic investors may absorb some of that selling. That does not make India immune to global events. US interest rates, the dollar, oil prices and international risk sentiment remain important.
But those external forces now interact with a deeper domestic financial system.
This is why Vyas argues that the broad label of “emerging markets” can sometimes hide more than it explains.
India, Brazil, Indonesia and South Africa may all sit within the same investment category, but their financial systems are very different. Their dependence on foreign capital, reserve positions, domestic savings, currency exposure and institutional depth can vary significantly.
Those differences become especially important when global borrowing conditions tighten.
For investors, this means that similar market movements may not always have the same meaning.
A decline in equities may indicate deteriorating economic fundamentals in one country. Somewhere else, it may simply reflect investors reallocating capital toward another opportunity.
A weaker currency may indicate financial stress, or it may represent an orderly adjustment to changing global interest rates.
The visible market movement is only the final result. Understanding what caused it requires looking underneath.
Capital does not move only because investors are worried
Another part of the discussion around international capital flows can also be misleading.
Money does not leave a country only because something has gone wrong there.
Sometimes another market has simply become more attractive.
If US assets begin offering better expected returns, global investors may shift capital toward the United States even when conditions in India or another emerging economy remain fundamentally sound.
This distinction is increasingly relevant as the United States encourages greater investment in manufacturing, technology and domestic production.
Under President Donald Trump, the focus on attracting investment and strengthening American productive capacity adds another variable to the international movement of capital.
From the perspective Vyas examines in his work, a stronger investment opportunity inside the United States can affect markets elsewhere without necessarily indicating weakness in those economies.
“Capital is continuously comparing opportunities,” Vyas said. “An outflow does not always mean investors have lost confidence. Sometimes another market has simply become more competitive.”
Geopolitics is changing where money goes
Monetary policy is also no longer the only major force determining international investment.
Trade policy, technology restrictions, supply-chain restructuring and geopolitical relationships increasingly influence where long-term capital is committed.
Vyas has examined this through his research on economic tensions between the United States and China.
Trade disputes involving strategic industries such as semiconductors are not only about imports and exports. They influence where companies build factories, where governments encourage investment and where investors expect future growth to emerge.
Capital often follows those decisions.
A technology company deciding where to establish manufacturing capacity can affect investment flows for years. A government encouraging domestic production can reshape supply chains. Restrictions on strategic technologies can influence which markets investors consider politically or commercially secure.
In that sense, global liquidity is becoming connected to a much broader set of forces.
Money is still moving internationally, but the routes available to it are becoming more selective.
A changing geography of liquidity
This has led Vyas to consider global liquidity less as a single pool of money and more as a changing geography of capital.
Financial markets remain highly interconnected.
A Federal Reserve announcement can affect Indian stocks within minutes. Oil-price movements can quickly influence inflation expectations. Political developments in one country can alter valuations on the other side of the world.
But being connected does not necessarily mean moving together.
The same global information can reach several markets simultaneously and still produce different outcomes because each economy processes that information through its own financial institutions, investor base and economic structure.
For India, this creates both opportunity and responsibility.
A larger domestic financial system can potentially reduce dependence on any single source of overseas capital. At the same time, remaining connected to international investment is important for economic growth and market development.
The challenge is therefore not to separate India from global finance, but to build a financial system capable of absorbing periods when global money becomes more selective.
From research to evaluating others’ research
Vyas’s work in finance and macroeconomics has also expanded beyond his own publications.
He has been involved in peer reviewing research across finance, economics and related areas, assessing methodology, empirical reasoning and whether conclusions are adequately supported by evidence.
Vyas has also taken on editorial and review responsibilities across several journals in finance, economics and related fields, where his work involves assessing research quality, methodology and the strength of the conclusions presented.
More recently, Vyas was selected as a member of the International Society of Managing and Technical Editors Board Nominating Committee, where he contributes to the review of candidates for senior Board positions.
He was recently elected as a Full Member of Sigma Xi, The Scientific Research Honour Society.
What this means for investors
The broader lesson from liquidity fragmentation is not that traditional indicators no longer matter. The Federal Reserve matters. The dollar matters. Bond yields and inflation matter. But investors increasingly need to understand the economy receiving those signals.
For India, that includes domestic savings, foreign-exchange reserves, energy dependence, institutional participation, foreign ownership and the depth of financial markets. The next major global shock may begin in Washington, Beijing or another financial centre. Its consequences, however, will depend on what it encounters when it reaches Mumbai.
Vyas’s research ultimately points toward a financial world that remains highly connected but increasingly less synchronized. Global money has not stopped moving. It is simply becoming more selective about where it goes, what risks it accepts and how long it stays.

articles.title: Higher ECB rates, tighter SME credit: the autumn outlook - DataDrivenInvestor
articles.summary: Higher ECB rates, tighter SME credit: the autumn outlook  DataDrivenInvestor
articles.full_text:
SMEs seeking financing may find it harder to secure a loan this autumn. Credit is expected to become more expensive, while approvals may become less common. This is largely a result of recent ECB tightening, even though the euro-area economy remains weak, with GDP growth forecast at just 0.9% for 2026. The reason for the tightening is an energy shock linked to the war in the Middle East, rather than an overheating economy. Because ECB rate decisions affect both the cost and availability of credit, some small businesses may start looking for alternative sources of financing.
What the ECB Actually Did
The ECB has raised its key rates twice this year, adding 25 basis points in June and another 25 in September. Since 16 September, the deposit facility rate has been 2.50%, the main refinancing rate 2.65% and the marginal lending rate 2.90%. For SMEs, this can translate into higher loan rates as banks pass increased funding costs on to borrowers and reassess the risk of new lending.
The September decision also raised the ECB’s inflation forecasts for the next two years. The 2026 forecast remained at 3.0%, while the projections for 2027 and 2028 increased from 2.3% to 2.5% and from 2.0% to 2.1%, respectively. Inflation influences how long those higher borrowing costs may persist. If price pressures remain elevated, the ECB has less room to ease policy, while banks may be more cautious about pricing and approving loans.
The policy rate is therefore only the first link in the chain: from the ECB to bank funding costs, from bank costs to lending conditions, and from lending conditions to whether an SME gets the financing it needs. That chain could tighten further if rates rise again. The next ECB meeting is on 29 October, and markets currently price in roughly a 58% chance of a move to 2.75%.
How a Rate Rise Reaches an SME Loan
An ECB rate rise reaches an SME loan through three channels:
- Price of Credit. Euribor and other market reference rates respond to changes in ECB policy, while banks adjust their lending rates as their own funding costs change. New loans and refinanced debt therefore become more expensive. For a floating-rate loan with a quarterly reset, a change in the reference rate can reach the borrower within three months.
- Bank Funding Conditions. Financial institutions also need to finance their own lending. In Q2 2026, euro-area banks reported weaker access to debt securities, money markets and retail deposits and expected further deterioration in Q3. More expensive or less available funding can put pressure on bank margins and limit the amount of credit banks are willing to supply, even when demand for loans remains strong.
- Loan Approvals. When funding becomes more constrained, banks can respond by tightening their lending criteria rather than simply raising interest rates. They may require more collateral, reduce the amount offered, or reject an application altogether.
The Squeeze Was Already Visible Before the Hikes
The pressure on SME financing was already building before the ECB’s September decision. In Q2 2026, 43% of SMEs reported a net increase in bank loan interest rates, up from 24% in Q1, according to the ECB’s SAFE survey. At the same time, the share of SMEs applying for bank loans rose from 17% to 19%, while the bank-loan financing gap remained negative. The data point to a market where demand for credit is holding up as borrowing conditions become less favourable.
Get Maclear AG’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.
Banks were also rejecting more corporate loan applications. In the Q2 Bank Lending Survey, the net share of banks reporting an increase in rejected applications for firms rose to 6%, from 3% in Q1. For SMEs, the figure was 7%. It was the highest reading for firms since Q4 2024. Banks also reported tighter credit standards and expected further tightening in Q3. The September rate hike adds pressure to a credit market that was already becoming more selective.
What It Means for Non-Bank Lenders and Investors
Higher rates create both an opportunity and a risk for non-bank lenders and investors. For lenders, they can result in higher yields on new loans. At the same time, SMEs facing more expensive bank credit may look for alternative financing, increasing the number of potential borrowers.
But higher rates also make those borrowers more expensive to finance. Interest payments take up a larger share of their cash flow, leaving less room to absorb weaker sales, rising costs, or other unexpected expenses. This increases the risk of missed payments and defaults.
The effect becomes more pronounced when banks tighten their lending criteria. To limit their own risk, banks can reduce loan amounts, require more collateral, or reject applications that no longer meet their internal requirements. This can push otherwise viable SMEs out of the banking system. A company may be rejected because its collateral is insufficient, its sector falls outside the bank’s preferred exposure, its loan is too small, or its required maturity does not fit the bank’s lending model. None of these factors necessarily means that the business itself is weak.
This changes the type of borrowers that reach non-bank lenders. Some will be companies that genuinely struggle to service debt. Others will be businesses that remain viable but no longer fit the criteria of traditional banks. Crowdlending platforms with strict due diligence, such as Maclear, can help investors distinguish between these cases by assessing the borrower and the specific loan before it is offered to investors.
Several principles can help reduce investor exposure to borrower risk. For instance, cash-flow analysis shows whether the business generates enough operating cash to cover interest and principal payments. Leverage and existing debt indicate how much additional borrowing the company can sustain. Collateral can provide a source of recovery if the borrower defaults, although its value depends on the type of asset, its liquidity, and the legal structure of the security. Loan-to-value limits can reduce exposure by keeping the loan amount below the assessed value of the collateral.
What to Watch Next
The next signals will come from both the ECB and the credit market. The ECB’s next rate decision is due on 29 October. The October Bank Lending Survey will show how banks changed credit standards, loan demand and rejection rates in Q3. The next SAFE survey will provide a broader view of how SMEs experienced changes in loan costs, availability and financing gaps. Together, these data will show whether tighter monetary policy is translating into a broader credit squeeze.

articles.summary: Jio Platforms IPO can be a re-rating trigger for Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel: Motilal Oswal  CNBC TV18Ambani's Jio Platforms plans to launch IPO on October 21, sources say  ReutersJio Platforms IPO may come without offer-for-sale, could value company at Rs 12 lakh crore  Telegraph IndiaRIL shares surge 2.7% on Jio Platforms IPO expectations, Jefferies boost  Moneycontrol.comJio IPO SWOT analysis: What the DRHP says about its growth story, moats and ...
articles.full_text:
2 Min Read
Brokerage firm Motilal Oswal has reiterated its 'Buy' rating on both Bharti Airtel and Reliance Industries (RIL), citing a compelling risk-reward profile for the two stocks.
The brokerage has a price target of ₹2,250 for Bharti Airtel and ₹1,530 for RIL.
The proposed initial public offering of Jio Platforms (JPL) could emerge as a key re-rating catalyst for both stocks, particularly Bharti Airtel. According to Bloomberg, Jio Platforms is reportedly seeking a valuation of around ₹11 lakh crore ($114 billion), broadly in line with Motilal Oswal's estimate of ₹11.2 lakh crore.
Motilal Oswal sees limited justification for Bharti Airtel trading at a significant discount to Jio. In addition to its core telecom operations, Bharti offers exposure to Indus Towers, Airtel Africa, data centres through Nxtra and financial services through Airtel Money, the brokerage said.
For RIL, the listing of Jio Platforms could provide greater visibility on the value of its telecom and digital business. RIL currently owns a 66.4% stake in JPL. While this stake could attract a holding-company discount after listing, Motilal Oswal believes the market is already factoring in a discount of around 18-36%.
The brokerage expects the telecom sector to see a tariff increase, with analysts building in a 15% hike in smartphone tariffs in December 2026.
The delay in tariff hikes has weighed on both Bharti Airtel and RIL, with the stocks down 15% and 23%, respectively, year-to-date, compared with a 13% decline in the Nifty.
However, the proposed Jio Platforms IPO and Vodafone Idea's impending fundraising could strengthen the case for a tariff hike, according to Motilal Oswal.
A Jio Platforms listing at a valuation of around ₹11 lakh crore could also help narrow the valuation gap between Bharti Airtel and Jio, the brokerage said.
Shares of RIL settled 2.49% higher at ₹1,216 on Tuesday, while Bharti Airtel ended 1.35% higher at ₹1,804.

articles.title: US Midterms: Frustrated voters, Trump’s low interest rate push and Fed’s stoic stance - https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.summary: US Midterms: Frustrated voters, Trump’s low interest rate push and Fed’s stoic stance  https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.full_text:
On September 17, Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh, the political appointee of Donald Trump, appeared in front of the American media with news that the White House would not have liked to hear: an increase in the benchmark overnight interest rate to the 3.75%-4.00% range.
Trump, during his presidential campaign two years back, had promised to lower prices on his watch. However, the combined impact of his global tariffs, an energy shock following the Iran war, and capital spending from the AI boom has kept price pressures intense enough.
Warsh, who called the rate hike a “right decision,” spoke in favour of a tighter monetary policy for an economy he sees as picking up speed.
For the new Fed boss, strong economic and job growth are adding to price pressures that no longer seem rooted in oil costs or import tariffs alone.
Troubled Trump didn’t like Warsh’s decision
Ironically, the rate increase became the first such move in three years and the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after being selected by Trump with an expectation that he would cut rates.
An angry Trump reacted by repeating what has been a standing call since returning to office in January 2025 that interest rates in the world’s largest economy should be slashed to perhaps 1%, a level usually associated with Fed efforts to boost the economy out of a crisis, especially during inflation times.
Trump clashed with former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, an episode that saw the Republican launching routine verbal attacks at the celebrated banking figure, who served during Trump 1.0 and the reign of Democrat Joe Biden. The clash ended up with Warsh replacing Powell.
And it looks like Warsh is following Powell’s footsteps by maintaining the stance that inflation would not improve at an adequate pace without tighter monetary policy, a direct counter to Trump administration officials’ comments that inflation was no longer a problem or would fall on its own over time.
The timing of the Fed rate hike couldn’t have been worse for Trump 2.0, as it will face the politically crucial midterm elections, a phenomenon that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the US Congress until the presidential elections of 2029.
As per the various surveys and projections, voters are already angry about high gasoline prices and interest rates on home mortgages.
While Fed policymakers, in their latest meeting, marked up their inflation estimates, guided by the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, to 3.7% versus the 3.6% projected at the June meeting, they don’t see inflation returning to the 2% target until 2029.
Talking about the Iran war, the US Congress’ Budget Office Accounting, a nonpartisan bookkeeper, came up with a damning report on September 15, in which it gave the figure of USD 38 billion as the cost paid by Uncle Sam so far in the conflict happening in the Middle East.
The office estimates that the amount will rise by USD 3 billion each month. The war is anticipated to raise the ratio by 0.5% during the first three months of 2027 in terms of inflation.
Let’s focus on the energy price front, a critical barometer of any country’s economic machinery.
There are three factors that are dominating the price shock right now: disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically important narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world’s oil travelled before the war, occasional attacks on the energy facilities in Iran’s neighbouring Gulf countries and Ukrainian strikes on Russia’s refineries, that is hurting the diesel landscape.
As global inventories struggle to prevent their stockpiles from going down, the effect has been seen on the price front, with consumers feeling the pain all over the world.
In the United States, states have been forced to take steps to curb diesel and gasoline prices. According to data from the American Automobile Association (AAA), diesel hit a record of USD 6.53 a gallon around the last week of September.
The White House is reportedly considering regulatory relief that would allow broader sales of red-dyed diesel, a move that could allow some buyers to avoid the federal fuel tax.
Trump, speaking on the issue, said that he won’t mind backing a ban on diesel exports. Red-dyed diesel is generally reserved for off-road uses such as farming and is exempt from most federal fuel taxes.
The US Department of Energy will offer another 40 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) in its bid to pull down the gasoline and diesel prices that have remained elevated nearly seven months into the Iran war.
The SPR ended August with 286.6 million barrels after another 3.1 million barrels left the reserve during the week ending August 28. That left the reserve well over 445 million barrels below maximum capacity.
Geopolitics hammering the US economy
The Congress Budget Office Accounting sees the rising cost of the Iran war potentially deteriorating the fiscal health of the world’s largest economy. The nation’s total public debt surpassed USD 40 trillion in August.
In the lead-up to the Iran war, the United States was witnessing a sort of recovery, with inflation standing at 2.4% in January, down from 2.7% in December 2025. Consumer buying power was also improving.
Then came the US-Israel joint strikes on Tehran, and nothing has been okay since then.
Trump said that the war would prove a “short-term excursion.” However, eight months on, no solution is in place. According to a segment of the American media, Trump is aiming for a significant peace deal in November, just days before the midterms, to gain political advantages.
But here is the brute reality: the economy will determine if Republicans keep control of Congress.
As per the Census Bureau’s September data, the US poverty rate edged down to the lowest on record in 2025, while median household income hit a record high.
As per the department, the decline marked the second consecutive annual drop in the poverty rate and brought it to its lowest level since the bureau began tracking the measure.
And here comes the most important figure: The poverty rate—the percentage of people living in poverty—dipped 0.5 percentage points to 10.2% last year.
Trump and Republicans will most probably use the data to present their side of the economy debate, but here is the comical tragedy: The same president, who, during his campaign, promised to “Make America Great Again,” and managed to do it to some extent on the poverty front, undid things himself by plunging into a geopolitical conflict.
The conflict has resulted in fuel price shock, inflation, and rising borrowing costs and mortgage rates.
In March, 35% of respondents to an NBC News poll said Trump had helped the economy. That number had dropped to only 26% by September.
Where things stand now
The August inflation numbers are out, and the increase was slower than expected. Price pressures, on the other hand, were more moderate in the prior month than previously reported, likely reducing the urgency for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in October.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCE) rose 0.3% after a downwardly revised 0.1% gain in July. Along with that, a sharp 4.4% rise in gasoline prices has kept inflation in the higher territory.
In the 12 months through August, PCE inflation advanced 3.4% after increasing by a downwardly revised 3.4% in July.
As per New York Fed President John Williams, the odds of an October rate hike were less, with the senior official seeing “no urgency” for further action.
A survey from the Conference Board showed consumer confidence plummeting to a near 12-1/2-year low in September, due to higher inflation and borrowing costs.
However, the same consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the US’ economic activity, surged 0.9% in August.
Annual revisions to the BEA (Bureau of Economic Analysis) data showed households having more savings than previously estimated as well as a higher income profile, explaining the resilience in consumer spending.
But here is another data point that undoes the gain: a modest 0.2% income rise in August. Disposable income was flat after adjusting for inflation. The saving rate dropped to 4.1%, the lowest level since November 2022, from 4.6% in July.
“We remain cautious that as real labour incomes slow with higher gas prices, there remain headwinds to spending in coming months,” said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup, while interacting with Reuters.
Even if the apex monetary body, in its October 27-28 meeting, decides to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged, that would serve no purpose for Trump, as the ratio will be at the current 3.75%-4.00% range.
Sifting through the numbers
On September 30, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis published its third estimate of Q2 GDP, as per which Uncle Sam grew at a “solid clip,” driven by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure.
Q2 GDP increased at a 2.2% annualised rate, revised up from the previously estimated 1.5% pace. In the previous quarter, the economy grew at a 2.5% rate.
When BEA analyzed the data, it came out with the conclusion: The economy has so far been able to hold up in the face of the disruptions caused by the Iran war, especially on the energy front, as businesses have been aggressively investing in AI. Furthermore, generous tax refunds from 2025’s tax legislation were underpinning consumer spending as well.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the American economy, grew at a 3.8% rate last quarter, revised up from the previously reported 3.4% pace.
Even as consumers continue to spend, household budgets have increasingly come under strain as well because of higher inflation and gasoline prices.

articles.title: Economist says fall harvest offers opportunity to gain information before choosing a federal farm program - Farm Talk
articles.summary: Economist says fall harvest offers opportunity to gain information before choosing a federal farm program  Farm Talk
articles.full_text:
Kansas farmers may have more time than they think to decide which federal farm program will provide their best fit for the 2026 crop, and a Kansas State University agricultural economist is encouraging producers to use that extra time.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Farm Service Agency announced that election and enrollment for the 2026 crop year will run from Sept. 16 through Dec. 11. The election and enrollment period for the 2027 crop year will run from Nov. 2 through March 15, 2027.
K-State Extension farm economist Robin Reid said the Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs provide income protection based on revenue or commodity prices. Producers can choose ARC-County or PLC on a crop-by-crop basis, and make different decisions on different FSA farm numbers.
According to Reid, the delayed 2026 decision deadline gives farmers an unusual opportunity to have more information about their crop before making their election.
“There is a real advantage this year by harvesting this crop before we are required to make the ARC/PLC decision,” Reid said. “Especially on wheat base, the marketing year has already started and we have a couple of prices already published from USDA.”
Other crops have just begun their marketing years, Reid said, but price estimates are available.
The timing of the decision could make this year's harvest particularly useful in evaluating ARC and PLC. If relatively high grain prices persist through the marketing year, Reid said, the choice could depend largely on county yields.
“If there were dry conditions during the growing season and lower yields across the county, ARC might be the way to go because it will pay even at higher prices since it is a revenue-based program,” Reid said.
Conversely, if county yields are above average, ARC would require a lower price to generate a payment, potentially making PLC more relevant, Reid said. Farmers should use their own individual farm information when comparing the programs, however.
“Farmers need to run the numbers for their individual farm,” Reid said. “As each farm has its’ own established program yield with FSA, that will determine how large PLC payments would be in relation to potential ARC payments”
K-State has developed an online spreadsheet to help producers evaluate potential ARC and PLC payments. The tool compares payment levels under different marketing-year average prices and is designed to help farmers examine the tradeoffs between the programs. A tutorial video and highlights from the video also are available through AgManager.info, a website maintained by the K-State Department of Agricultural Economics.
Reid said farmers should begin considering their options but do not need to immediately visit their local FSA office.
“As many have started or will soon be starting harvest, I would encourage farmers to be thinking about the decision but there is no need to rush into the local FSA office at this time,” she said. “Get through harvest and evaluate how yields turned out, and then do the election and enrollment.”
Reid also encouraged producers not to wait until the deadline because FSA offices could face heavy workloads and staffing constraints.
The USDA announcement also included an update on new base acres, which farmers could qualify for if they were planting more acres than they had in base. More than 30 million acres were eligible for new base-acre allocations, exceeding the national cap. As a result, FSA applied a 3.69% reduction to newly allocated base acres. Existing base acres are not affected, according to Reid.
Meanwhile, ARC and PLC payments for the 2025 crop are scheduled to begin in October 2026. As a result of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, farmers will receive the higher of the calculated ARC or PLC payment for that crop year, regardless of the program they elected.
Reid said corn, soybeans, wheat and grain sorghum will receive PLC payments for 2025, although ARC payments are higher in some cases for corn and soybeans. K-State shows estimates for these payments for farmers to use on their cash flow.
For the 2026 crop, Reid said producers can use the harvest results, available price information and K-State's decision tools to make a more informed election before the Dec. 11 deadline. K-State’s Department of Agricultural Economics will also be having informational webinars as the deadline gets closer.

articles.full_text:
The dollar index DXY is down by -0.24% today, falling back from Monday’s 1.5-year high. The widening of the US Aug trade deficit to a 17-month high is bearish for the dollar. Also, today’s -1% decline in WTI crude oil to a 1-month low eases inflation expectations and could potentially persuade the Fed to loosen monetary policy, a negative factor for the dollar. In addition, today’s rally in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 to new all-time highs has reduced demand for dollar liquidity.
The US Aug trade deficit increased to a 17-month high of -$105.6 billion, wider than expectations of -$102.1 billion and likely to weigh on Q3 GDP.
